fact: SRW Products says its Seams Right turf seam adhesive bonds properly only when surfaces are flat, completely dry and above 40°F and free of moisture or frost, and that turf must be protected from rain and freezing for 12 hours after installation, from light foot traffic for 12 hours and heavy traffic for 24; full cure takes 24 to 48 hours.
quote: For proper adhesion surfaces must be flat, completely dry, and above 40°F. Make sure the surfaces being bonded are clean of any materials that may prevent proper adhesion like dust, loose turf fibers, moisture, or frost. … Protect turf from rain/water and freezing conditions for 12 hours after installation. Protect from light foot traffic for 12 hours, and heavy foot traffic for 24 hours. … CURE TIME • 60-120 minutes, full cure 24-48 hours.
source_label: SRW Products, Seams Right Turf Adhesive (product page and technical data sheet)
notes: Same wording on the product page and the linked technical data sheet (srwproducts.com/wp-content/uploads/SeamsRightAdhesive_TDS-1.pdf), both read 2026-09-25. One manufacturer; other adhesives set other limits (see the TEC 149 record).

fact: SRW Products tells installers to peel back a seam just before gluing, because turf backing can heat up and expand and leave gaps at the seam when it cools, and says its adhesive will freeze or be damaged by low temperatures in storage.
quote: Peel back seam just before applying adhesive to tape. The turf backing can heat up and expand, leaving unwanted gaps at seams when the turf cools. … Store at room temperature, no freezing weather. Will freeze or be damaged by low temperatures.
source_label: SRW Products, Seams Right Turf Adhesive (product page and technical data sheet)

fact: TEC Specialty Products' data sheet for its TEC 149 two-part turf adhesive says the adhesive, the air, the base and the turf should all be between 59°F and 84°F, that lower temperatures prolong curing and higher ones shorten working time, and that it should not be applied in wet, rainy or misty conditions.
quote: The temperature of adhesive, environment, field base and synthetic turf field covering should be between 59°F and 84°F (15°C and 29°C). … Lower temperatures negatively influence the consistency of the adhesive, thus prolonging the curing time. … Higher temperatures shorten the adhesive pot life and application time. … Adhesive should not be applied in wet, raining and misty conditions.
source_label: TEC Specialty Products, TEC 149 2-C Turf Adhesive product data sheet (updated March 2026)
notes: A sports-field adhesive sold in summer and winter formulas; the data sheet says it is valid for 90 days from its date, so re-read it before relying on the range.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, a turf supplier, says cold seam edges are stiff and make a good seam harder, that a heater may be needed in freezing weather so turf can lie flat without being stretched hard, that many hardware-store seam adhesives are water-based and may freeze, and that turf rolls should be stored so freezing temperatures do not leave flat spots, turning a roll now and then if it has to sit outside.
quote: When seaming in cold weather, the two edges that are to be seamed may be stiff/hard and achieving a successful seam will be more difficult. … Roll out your synthetic turf and allow it to lay flat on the prepped surface to remove any wrinkles. In freezing temperatures you may need to have an external heater available to expedite this process. This will make your installation more efficient and prevent aggressively stretching the turf to reach its flatness on the compacted subgrade. … a majority of hardware store adhesives are water based and contain high percentages of fillers. These inexpensive water-based adhesives may freeze under cold weather conditions … Always store your rolls of synthetic grass so the freezing temperatures will not leave flat spots in the turf roll. If you have to store the turf outside, rotate the roll occasionally to prevent flat spots from occurring.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Cold Weather Artificial Grass Installation
notes: A supplier's installer column; it also promotes the supplier's own adhesive, which the guide does not repeat.

fact: Synthetic Grass Warehouse says the turf surface must be dry when infill is spread, because infill sticks to damp blades instead of reaching the base of the fibers, and turf expands and contracts as the temperature rises through the day.
quote: When placing the infill the surface must be dry in order for the infill to reach the base of the fibers. If the surface has any moisture the infill will stick to the top and will have to dry out or be removed to complete this process. … With the rise in temperature throughout the day, the synthetic turf will expand and/or contract.
source_label: Synthetic Grass Warehouse, Ask JW: Cold Weather Artificial Grass Installation

fact: The street standards Larimer County, Loveland and Fort Collins share bar work on subgrade in freezing conditions or when it is frozen, and bar placing base course on soft, spongy or frozen subgrade.
quote: 22.5.2 C. 1. Preparation Conditions. Work shall not occur on the subgrade in freezing conditions, or when the subgrade is frozen. … 22.5.4 D. … No base course shall be placed upon a soft, spongy, or frozen subgrade or other subgrade, the stability of which, in the opinion of the Local Entity Engineer, is unsuitable.
source_label: Larimer County Urban Area Street Standards, Chapter 22: Materials and Construction Specifications (repealed and reenacted Aug. 1, 2021; adopted by Larimer County, Loveland and Fort Collins)
notes: Street and right-of-way standards, not a rule for private yards; the guide uses them only as the local engineering practice on frozen and soft ground. larimer.gov answers plain curl with a Cloudflare 403; read 2026-09-25 through a fetch that passed. Page footer: "Larimer County Urban Area Street Standards – Repealed and Reenacted August 1, 2021 Adopted by Larimer County, City of Loveland, City of Fort Collins".

fact: When ice in the ground melts, the water cannot drain out of the soil fast enough, so the soil becomes substantially weaker and loses bearing capacity; engineers call this thaw weakening.
quote: Thaw weakening. A weakened subgrade condition resulting from soil saturation as ice within the soil melts. … As the ice melts and turns to liquid it cannot drain out of the soil fast enough and thus the subgrade becomes substantially weaker (less stiff) and tends to lose bearing capacity.
source_label: Pavement Interactive, Frost Action (reference desk)

fact: CSU Extension says soils compact more easily when wet, that clayey soil should never be worked wet, and that a squeezed handful that only reshapes instead of crumbling is too wet; on some clay soils only a few days, or hours, separate too wet from too dry, and frequent spring rains can delay work significantly.
quote: Soils are more prone to compaction when wet. Soil water acts as a lubricant allowing the soil particles to readily slide together reducing large pore spaces. … Never cultivate clayey soil when wet, as this will destroy soil structure; the clods created by tilling wet clay may last for years. To check dryness, take a handful of soil and gently squeeze it into a ball. If the soil is dry enough to crumble, it may be cultivated. If the ball only reshapes with pressure, it is too wet for cultivation. On some clayey soils, there may be only a few days (or even hours) between the time when the soil is too wet and too dry (too hard) to cultivate. In years when frequent spring rains prevent the soil from drying, planting will be significantly delayed.
source_label: CSU Extension, CMG GardenNotes #215: Soil Compaction
notes: Written for gardens and cultivation; the guide applies it to digging and compacting a turf base on clay, which is an inference and is worded as such.

fact: CSU Extension's PlantTalk Colorado says sod can go in through the growing season but its roots should be well established before fall freezes, and new sod should be kept moist until it roots, within two to three weeks.
quote: You can install sod throughout the growing season, anytime good quality sod is available, and you have prepared the soil to help roots become established as quickly as possible. Roots should be well established before freezing temperatures in the fall. … Water your newly sodded lawn frequently enough to keep the sod and underlying soil moist, not soggy. Sod should be well rooted into the soil below within two to three weeks.
source_label: CSU Extension, PlantTalk Colorado 1517: Sodding a Lawn

fact: Johnstown's 2026 New Lawn Permit says no new lawn may be established after October 15, whatever the permit, that watering after October 15 is limited to hand-watering trees and shrubs, and that applications are open until October 12, 2026.
quote: New Lawn Permit Application - Available until October 12th, 2026 … All watering is restricted to hand watering only of trees and shrubs after October 15th regardless of permit status. I understand the New Turf Permit guidelines and regardless of the permit, no turf establishment shall occur after October 15th.
source_label: Town of Johnstown, 2026 New Lawn Permit (Municipal Code Sec. 13-151(c)(6))
notes: "Turf" on this page means a live lawn (sod or seed); the rule says nothing about artificial turf. The same page quotes Sec 13-151.(c)(6) and says a permit expires 45 days after installation or at the end of the mandated watering schedule.
